name: Callotasis (callus distraction)

card.summary: A surgical method that cuts a bone and slowly pulls the ends apart so new bone grows in the gap, used in limb lengthening and, in the same family of technique, in jaw advancement for appearance.
card.note: Major surgery with a long treatment period and documented complications.

quick.overview:
Callotasis, or callus distraction, is a bone-lengthening technique. A surgeon cuts the bone, fixes it with an external or internal device, and the segments are then separated gradually so new bone forms between them. The result is a longer bone.

For looks, it is the principle behind height-increase limb lengthening and related jaw procedures, where more bone means more height or a more projecting face. It has been used clinically since the early twentieth century for unequal leg length and reconstruction, and a large published literature exists.
quick.how: The procedure runs in phases: a surgical cut, a latency period of about a week, a distraction phase at roughly 1 mm a day, and a consolidation phase while the new bone hardens, after which the device is removed in a second operation. It is done by specialist orthopaedic or maxillofacial surgeons.
quick.risks: Reported complications include infection (about 5%), bone growing in the wrong direction (7 to 9%), hardware failure and, in jaw surgery, nerve damage. Separating too slowly risks premature union and too quickly risks nonunion. It involves months of recovery.

lead: Callotasis, also called callus distraction, is a form of distraction osteogenesis: surgeons cut a bone, attach a device and gradually separate the ends so that new bone, formed from the callus in the gap, lengthens the bone.[1]

For appearance, the technique is relevant as the underlying mechanism of cosmetic limb lengthening for height and of jaw lengthening procedures. It is otherwise used for unequal leg length, short fingers and toes, and facial deformities.[1][2]

The technique was reported in clinical use in 1905 by Alessandro Codivilla and later developed extensively by Gavriil Ilizarov from the 1950s.[1] The literature on it includes clinical trials, reviews and animal studies.

chain: Bone is cut and a device attached
Segments separated gradually; new bone fills the gap
A longer bone, adding height or jaw projection
angle.text: Callotasis lengthens bone itself, which is why it underlies surgical height-increase and jaw-lengthening procedures. It is performed in hospital by specialist surgeons.

paras: After the bone cut, the device is left inactive for about seven days of latency while early healing begins. Distraction then separates the segments at about 1 mm a day, usually in two steps, and a consolidation phase holds the bone stable until it heals fully. A second operation removes the device.[1]

Bernhard von Langenbeck proposed the idea in 1869, and Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, treating 26 people with malformed legs; complication rates were high and his methods were not adopted.[1] Ilizarov studied the method in more than 15,000 people from the 1950s, developed external fixation devices and established separation rates, leading to wide use.[1] Use on the jaw was pioneered by Wolfgang Rosenthal in 1930, with modern clinical reports from 1992.[1]

Callotasis was originally used for unequal leg length and, since the 1980s, for facial conditions such as hemifacial microsomia and micrognathism.[1] Reviews describe it for short toes and metatarsals (brachymetatarsia), femoral lengthening in children, and metacarpal lengthening in brachydactyly.[3][4][5]

Infection occurs in about 5% overall, bone growing in the wrong direction in 7 to 9%, hardware failure in 3 to 4.5%, and protocol errors in about 4.5%; inferior alveolar nerve damage occurs in 3.5% of mandibular distractions.[1]

Clinical trials have examined callotasis for correcting genu recurvatum with the Ilizarov method,[6] metacarpal lengthening in childhood brachydactyly,[7] and bone mineralization at the distraction site after lengthening.[8] A terminated registered trial studied an intramedullary system for leg length inequality.[9] These studies concern medical indications, not cosmetic height.
